title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: After the execution, Pierre was separated from the rest of the prisoners and placed alone in a small, ruined, and filthy church.

Toward evening a noncommissioned officer entered with two soldiers and told him that he had been pardoned and would now go to the barracks for prisoners of war. Without understanding what was said to him, Pierre got up and went with the soldiers. They took him to the upper end of the field, where there were some sheds built of charred planks, beams, and scraps of wood, and led him into one of them. In the darkness some twenty different men surrounded Pierre. He looked at them without understanding who they were, why they were there, or what they wanted. He heard what they said but did not grasp the meaning of the words and drew no kind of conclusions from them. He replied to questions they put to him but did not consider who was listening or how they would understand his replies. He looked at their faces and figures, but they all seemed equally meaningless to him.

From the moment Pierre had witnessed those terrible murders committed by men who did not wish to commit them, it was as if the mainspring of his life, on which everything depended and which made everything appear alive, had suddenly been wrenched out and everything had collapsed into a heap of meaningless debris. Though he did not acknowledge it to himself, his faith in the right ordering of the universe, in humanity, in his own soul, and in God had been destroyed. He had experienced this before, but never so powerfully. Previously, when similar doubts had assailed him, they had been the result of his own wrongdoing, and at the bottom of his heart he had felt that relief from despair and doubt was to be found within himself. But now he felt that the universe had crumbled before his eyes and only meaningless ruins remained—and this through no fault of his own. He felt that it was not in his power to regain faith in the meaning of life.

Around him in the darkness men were standing, and evidently something about him interested them greatly. They were telling him something and asking him something. Then they led him away somewhere, and at last he found himself in a corner of the shed among men who were laughing and talking on all sides.
"Well, then, mates... that very prince who..." some voice at the other end of the shed was saying, with a strong emphasis on the word who.

Sitting silent and motionless on a heap of straw against the wall, Pierre sometimes opened and sometimes closed his eyes. But as soon as he closed them he saw before him the dreadful face of the factory boy—especially dreadful because of its simplicity—and the faces of the murderers, even more dreadful because of their unease. And he opened his eyes again and stared blankly into the darkness around him.

Beside him, in a stooping position, sat a small man whose presence Pierre first became aware of through a strong smell of sweat that came from him every time he moved. This man was doing something to his legs in the darkness, and though Pierre could not see his face, he sensed that the man kept glancing at him. Growing accustomed to the darkness, Pierre saw that the man was taking off his leg wrappings, and the way he did it aroused Pierre's interest.

Having unwound the string that tied the wrapping on one leg, he carefully coiled it up and immediately set to work on the other leg, glancing up at Pierre. While one hand hung up the first string, the other was already unwinding the wrapping on the second leg. In this way, having carefully removed the leg wrappings with deft circular motions of his arm following one another without interruption, the man hung them up on some pegs fixed above his head. Then he took out a knife, cut something, closed the knife, placed it under the head of his bed, and seating himself comfortably, clasped his arms around his raised knees and fixed his eyes on Pierre. Pierre was conscious of something pleasant, comforting, and well-rounded in these deft movements, in the man's well-ordered arrangements in his corner, and even in his very smell, and he looked at the man without taking his eyes off him.
"You've seen a lot of trouble, sir, haven't you?" the little man suddenly said.

And there was so much kindness and simplicity in his singsong voice that Pierre tried to reply, but his jaw trembled and he felt tears rising to his eyes. The little fellow, giving Pierre no time to show his emotion, instantly continued in the same pleasant tones:

"Eh, lad, don't fret!" said he, in the tender, singsong, caressing voice old Russian peasant women use. "Don't fret, friend—'suffer an hour, live for a lifetime!' That's how it is, my dear fellow. And here we live, thank God, without offense. Among these folk too there are good men as well as bad," said he, and still speaking, he turned on his knees with a supple movement, got up, coughed, and went off to another part of the shed.
"Hey, you rascal!" Pierre heard the same kind voice saying at the other end of the shed. "So you've come back, you rascal? She remembers... Now, now, that'll do!"
And the soldier, pushing away a little dog that was jumping up at him, returned to his place and sat down. In his hands he had something wrapped in a rag.
"Here, have a bite, sir," said he, resuming his former respectful tone as he unwrapped and offered Pierre some baked potatoes. "We had soup for dinner and the potatoes are wonderful!"
Pierre had not eaten all day, and the smell of the potatoes seemed extremely pleasant. He thanked the soldier and began to eat.
"Well, are they all right?" said the soldier with a smile. "You should try it this way."
He took a potato, drew out his clasp knife, cut it into two equal halves on the palm of his hand, sprinkled some salt on it from the rag, and handed it to Pierre.
"The potatoes are wonderful!" he said once more. "Try some like that!"
Pierre thought he had never eaten anything that tasted better.
"Oh, I'm all right," said he, "but why did they shoot those poor men? The last one was barely twenty."

"Tsk, tsk..." said the little man. "Ah, what a sin... what a sin!" he added quickly, and as if his words were always waiting ready in his mouth and flew out of their own accord, he went on: "How is it, sir, that you stayed in Moscow?"
"I didn't think they would come so soon. I stayed by accident," replied Pierre.
"And how did they arrest you, dear fellow? At your house?"
"No, I went to look at the fire, and they arrested me there and tried me as an arsonist."
"Where there's law, there's injustice," put in the little man.
"And have you been here long?" Pierre asked, munching the last of the potato.
"Me? It was last Sunday they took me, out of a hospital in Moscow."
"Why, are you a soldier then?"
"Yes, we are soldiers of the Apsheron regiment. I was dying of fever. We weren't told anything. There were some twenty of us lying there. We had no idea, never guessed at all."
"And do you feel sad here?" Pierre asked.

"How can one not feel sad, lad? My name is Platon, and the surname is Karataev," he added, evidently wanting to make it easier for Pierre to address him. "They call me 'little falcon' in the regiment. How can one not feel sad? Moscow—she's the mother of cities. How can one see all this and not feel sad? But 'the worm gnaws the cabbage, yet dies first'; that's what the old folks used to tell us," he added quickly.
"What? What did you say?" asked Pierre.
"Who? Me?" said Karataev. "I say things happen not as we plan but as God decides," he replied, thinking he was repeating what he had said before, and immediately continued:
"Well, and you, sir, do you have an estate? And a house? So you're well-off, then? And a wife? And are your old parents still living?" he asked.

And though it was too dark for Pierre to see, he felt that a suppressed smile of kindliness puckered the soldier's lips as he asked these questions. He seemed saddened that Pierre had no parents, especially no mother.
"A wife for counsel, a mother-in-law for welcome, but there's none so dear as one's own mother!" said he. "Well, and do you have little ones?" he went on asking.
Again Pierre's negative answer seemed to distress him, and he hastened to add:
"Never mind! You're young folks yet, and God willing you may still have some. The main thing is to live in harmony..."
"But it's all the same now," Pierre could not help saying.
"Ah, my dear fellow!" replied Karataev. "Never refuse a prison cell or a beggar's sack!"
He settled himself more comfortably and coughed, evidently preparing to tell a long story.

"Well, my dear fellow, I was still living at home," he began. "We had a prosperous homestead, plenty of land; we peasants lived well and our house was one to thank God for. When Father and we went out mowing, there were seven of us. We lived well. We were real peasants. It so happened..."
And Platon Karataev told a long story of how he had gone into someone's woods to take firewood, how he had been caught by the gamekeeper, was tried, flogged, and sent to serve as a soldier.

"Well, lad," and a smile changed the tone of his voice, "we thought it was a misfortune but it turned out a blessing! If it hadn't been for my sin, my brother would have had to go as a soldier. But he, my younger brother, had five little ones, while I, you see, only left a wife behind. We had a little girl, but God took her before I went as a soldier. I came home on leave and I'll tell you how it was—I look and see that they're living better than before. The yard full of livestock, the women at home, two brothers away earning wages, and only Mikhail, the youngest, at home. Father said, 'All my children are the same to me: it hurts the same whichever finger gets bitten. But if Platon hadn't been shaved for a soldier, Mikhail would have had to go.' He called us all before the icons. 'Mikhail,' he says, 'come here and bow at his feet; and you, young woman, bow down too; and you, grandchildren, also bow before him! Do you understand?' he says. That's how it is, dear fellow. Fate looks for a head. But we are always judging, 'that's not right, this isn't fair!' Our luck is like water in a net: you pull and it bulges, but when you've drawn it out, it's empty! That's how it is."
And Platon shifted his seat on the straw.
After a short silence he rose.
"Well, I think you must be sleepy," said he, and began rapidly crossing himself, repeating:

"Lord Jesus Christ, holy Saint Nicholas, Frola and Lavra! Lord Jesus Christ, holy Saint Nicholas, Frola and Lavra! Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on us and save us!" he concluded, then bowed to the ground, got up, sighed, and sat down again on his heap of straw. "That's the way. Lay me down like a stone, O God, and raise me up like a loaf," he muttered as he lay down, pulling his coat over himself.
"What prayer was that you were saying?" asked Pierre.
"Eh?" murmured Platon, who had almost fallen asleep. "What was I saying? I was praying. Don't you pray?"
"Yes, I do," said Pierre. "But what was that you said: Frola and Lavra?"

"Well, of course," replied Platon quickly, "the horses' saints. One must have pity on the animals too. Hey, you rascal! Now you've curled up and got warm, you daughter of a..." said Karataev, touching the dog that lay at his feet, and again turning over, he fell asleep immediately.

Sounds of crying and screaming came from somewhere in the distance outside, and flames were visible through the cracks of the shed, but inside it was quiet and dark. For a long time Pierre did not sleep but lay with eyes open in the darkness, listening to the steady snoring of Platon beside him, and he felt that the world that had been shattered was once more stirring in his soul with a new beauty and on new and unshakable foundations.
